sections.title: Audit a draft
sections.intro: A friend asks you to review their written answer to "Tell me about a challenging project" before their interview. Go through it the way the self-audit checklist does.

questions.prompt: Their draft spends 80% of its length on the system architecture. What's the first problem?
options: It's fine — technical depth always scores well
It misses what's being assessed — "challenging" means Perseverance
It's too short — architecture needs even more depth
It should open with the architecture diagram
questions.explanation: Pitfall #1. It feels safer to show competence than to talk about the hard part, but the hard part is what's being scored. Pause, name the signal being asked for, and then answer it.

questions.prompt: You count pronouns in their Actions:
questions.snippet: "We decided to use Redis. We built a new service. We shipped on time."
options: Fine — "I" would sound arrogant here
The "We" Disease — say what *they* decided and built
Good — it shows they're a team player
Too short — add more "we" detail
questions.explanation: The interviewer is evaluating them, not their team. "I proposed Redis because reads outnumbered writes 100:1" is precise about their part, and interviewers don't read precision as arrogance.

questions.snippet: "I built the filter and shipped it on time."
options: Not enough actions — no visible judgment or technique
Fine, if the Results section is strong
Perfect — concise and outcome-focused
Too much detail for an Actions section
questions.explanation: Pitfall #2. A chain like "found N+1 queries → rewrote them as a single JOIN → p95 went from 3.2s to 400ms → support tickets dropped 60%" shows how they work. One summary line shows nothing they could repeat.

questions.prompt: You time their Context read aloud: 75 seconds of team history and reporting lines. What do you suggest?
options: Cut to ~20 seconds — keep only the stakes
Keep it, but speak faster through it
Keep it — the history makes the stakes clear
Move the history to the end as a recap
questions.explanation: Pitfall #3: about 10% of the story. Interpersonal detail can earn its place in a conflict story, but only when it serves the Actions.

questions.snippet: "We shipped on time, the metrics went up, and everyone was thrilled."
options: Too negative — they should sound more excited
Ideal — a clean ending leaves a strong impression
A fairy tale ending — add the real obstacle or flaw
Fine, as long as the metrics are specific
questions.explanation: Pitfall #6. With no friction at all, it sounds like they weren't close to the real work, or like they're hiding something. A real obstacle also gives the Learnings something to land on.

questions.prompt: One line in their story says "my manager assigned me this project." They're interviewing for a senior role. Why flag it?
options: It invites an uncharitable read: "do they wait to be told?"
It's dishonest — they should say they chose it
It's fine — it shows they follow direction
It's too much org-chart detail
questions.explanation: Senior interviewers tend to fill gaps with negative assumptions. Thinking defensively means turning straight to what *you* did with the assignment, or leaving out the framing if it adds nothing.

questions.prompt: They say: "It's all written down, I know it cold, I don't need to say it out loud." Your response?
options: Agreed — written prep is enough
Practicing out loud is what makes delivery match the page
Reading it once more silently will do
They should memorize it word for word
questions.explanation: Pitfall #7. Candidates who've rehearsed out loud beat candidates with better material who haven't. Practice the key points, not exact wording, or it'll sound robotic.

sections.title: Spot the problem
sections.intro: Match the symptom to the pitfall, or the signal-area check that fails.

questions.prompt: A Staff-level candidate tells a conflict story about a disagreement with a peer over variable naming. Which check fails?
options: Involvement — they weren't central to it
Empathy — they made the peer look bad
Scope — a peer-level, low-stakes conflict reads junior
Relationship — the outcome isn't stated
questions.explanation: Conflict scope should match the target level. For Staff, look for disagreements with a manager, across orgs, or over system design and team charters.

questions.prompt: A senior candidate says: "I prioritized the roadmap and we hit our goals." What's missing?
options: Humility — they should credit the team
A metric — they need an exact percentage
Context — they need more team background
The framework — the criteria behind the prioritizing
questions.explanation: At senior levels and up, they want to see *how* you think, so they can tell whether your decision process would work in their org. Name the criteria and the trade-offs.

questions.prompt: A Leadership story covers only the candidate's own code. Which check fails?
options: It's fine — strong code is leadership by example
It needs a bigger team to count as leadership
It doesn't show how they enabled others to do good work
It's too technical for a Leadership question
questions.explanation: Leadership signal is about creating the conditions for others: mentoring, unblocking, building consensus. Say it explicitly. Don't leave it for the interviewer to infer.

questions.snippet: "My mistake was that I deleted the production database because I didn't know what a WHERE clause was."
options: Ideal — a big, honest mistake is the best Growth story
Too basic for the level — it raises maturity doubts
Too vague — it needs exact downtime numbers
Fine, as long as they say they're sorry
questions.explanation: The mistake should be real but not damaging to your credibility. Pick one that shows growth in skill, and ideally show the lesson applied later.

questions.prompt: A candidate's stories regularly run 5-6 minutes, with backtracking ("wait, before that…"). Most likely cause?
options: Stories that are too low in scope
Not enough out-loud practice
Too many "I" statements
Interviewers who ask too many questions
questions.explanation: Overlong answers, losing your place, tangents, filler words, and uneven pacing are all signs of too little rehearsal, not of weak material.

questions.prompt: An Ownership story ends with "…and then I handed it off to the other team." Which check fails?
options: Too recent — ownership stories should be older
Wrong signal — handoffs are Communication
Too much "I" — it sounds like they did it alone
No measured result — did the fix actually work?
questions.explanation: Ownership means driving it end-to-end, including checking that it worked and explaining why those metrics mattered. Flagging a problem and handing it off is only half the job.
